findings.summary: The page titled "Binary Search in Rotated Sorted Array" contains no rotated-array content at all — no definition, no pivot code, no sorted-half search — yet later pages depend on that material.
findings.evidence: page_title "Binary Search in Rotated Sorted Array", subtitle "One half is always sorted"; the blocks are a mountain-array diagram ("Find target = 4: not in [1,3,5,7], reverse BS finds index 5"), a generic `bs(...)` helper, "5. Search insert position", "3. Infinite sorted array", and a complexity table. Page 4 later asserts "Rotated Array (Find Target) | find target | identify sorted half, search in it" and page 2 warns "Forgetting boundary conditions in rotated arrays".
findings.fix: Restore the chapter 5 material on this page before anything else: the rotated-sorted-array definition ([1,2,3,4,5,6,7] -> [4,5,6,7,1,2,3]), the `findPivot` code with the arr[mid] > arr[high] reasoning, the `search` function showing which half is sorted, and the target = 2 dry run. Move the insert-position / infinite-array / complexity blocks to the advanced-patterns page where they belong.

findings.summary: "Peak" and "reverse BS" are used in the opening diagram and in the page 2 comparison table, but the peak-element and mountain-array sections that define them (findPeak, the mountain search procedure) never appear in this part.
findings.evidence: Page 1 diagram pointers: {"index":3,"label":"peak"} with caption "Find target = 4: not in [1,3,5,7], reverse BS finds index 5"; page 1 code note "asc false: flip the comparison"; page 2 table row ["Peak / Mountain","mountain array","not required","peak / target","Peak Element, Mountain"]; page 3 lists "13 Find Peak Element (Mountain Array)". No block anywhere defines a peak element or the three-step mountain search.
findings.fix: Add sections 1 and 2 of chapter 6 before the diagram: the peak definition plus the arr[mid] < arr[mid+1] rule and `findPeak` code, then the mountain search steps (find peak, normal BS on [0, peak], reverse BS on [peak+1, n-1]) that the `asc` flag and the "reverse BS finds index 5" caption depend on.

findings.summary: The pattern table gives the 2D-matrix precondition as "row & col sorted", which is the LeetCode-240 staircase problem (O(n+m)); the flatten-and-binary-search code and O(log(n·m)) bound on this deck require the strictly stronger "first of a row > last of the previous row".
findings.evidence: table row ["2D Matrix","row & col sorted","not required","target","search 2D matrix"] versus the bullet on the same page "First of a row > last of the previous row" and code "int low=0, high=R*n-1; ... int r = mid / n, c = mid % n;"
findings.fix: Change the search-space cell to "fully sorted when flattened (first of row > last of previous row)"; if the row-and-column-sorted variant is meant, add it as a separate row with staircase search and O(n + m).

findings.summary: The claim that both midpoint formulas give the same value is asserted unqualified immediately after bullets stating the unsafe form lands outside the array, and its proof and precondition appear only on the next page.
findings.evidence: Page 5 bullets: "The sum silently ==wraps== to a negative" / "mid then points outside the array", followed directly by "Both forms give the ==same midpoint==. Only the safe one never builds a value larger than `high`." Page 6 supplies the proof and the condition: "Both floor alike when 0 <= low <= high".
findings.fix: Qualify the page 5 sentence ("when no overflow occurs, both forms give the same midpoint") or move it above the overflow bullets, so the learner is not told the two forms agree one line after being told one of them goes negative.

findings.summary: The C/C++ advice to "cast to unsigned" is stated in a way that still leaves the signed addition undefined; the operands, not the sum, must be cast.
findings.evidence: bullet: "C / C++ have no `>>>`: cast to `unsigned` instead"
findings.fix: Spell out the operand cast: "C / C++ have no `>>>`: write ((unsigned)low + (unsigned)high) >> 1 — casting the sum is too late."

findings.summary: The closing "write the safe form always" advice is placed mid-page, ahead of the proof and the "where it bites" cases that justify it.
findings.evidence: Page 6 order: >>> bullets, then check bullets "Write the safe form **always**, by habit" / "Use `long` when bounds are still bigger", then "6. Same Midpoint, Proved", then "7. Where It Bites" and the long-bounds table.
findings.fix: Move the check-bullet advice block to the end of page 6, after section 7 and the bound-size table, so the recommendation follows its evidence.

findings.summary: The tip generalises the index trick to arbitrary averages, but for signed operands a + (b - a) / 2 can still overflow and does not equal (a + b) / 2 under truncating division.
findings.evidence: callout tip: "Same trick for averages: a + (b - a) / 2 instead of (a + b) / 2."
findings.fix: Qualify it: "Same trick for averages of **non-negative** values. For mixed signs, b - a can overflow too and truncation makes the two forms differ (a=-3, b=0 gives -1 vs -2) — widen to long or use Math.floorDiv(a + b, 2) on a wider type."
